title: Sensex Crashes 1,677 Points as Trump Declares Iran Deal 'Over' — Oil Surges, Rupee Hits One-Month Low
excerpt: Indian markets suffered their worst single-day fall in three months after the US-Iran ceasefire collapsed, sending Brent crude past $79, the rupee to 95.55, and the India VIX up 26 percent — a triple blow for NRI investors watching from abroad.
body:
Indian equity markets suffered their steepest single-day fall in over three months on Wednesday as US President Donald Trump declared the peace memorandum with Iran "over" at a NATO summit in Ankara, triggering a cascade of selling across global financial markets and sending crude oil prices soaring.

The BSE Sensex plunged 1,677 points, or 2.15 percent, to close at 76,503.60. The Nifty 50 dropped 516.65 points, or 2.12 percent, to settle at 23,882.05 — decisively breaching the 24,000 support level that analysts had flagged as critical. All 16 sectoral indices ended in the red, with financials, oil and gas, chemicals, and banking bearing the heaviest losses.

## What triggered the sell-off

The crash was set in motion by an escalation that unravelled weeks of fragile calm. After Iranian forces targeted US military sites in Bahrain and Kuwait — reportedly in response to attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz — US forces struck over 80 Iranian targets. Trump's declaration that the ceasefire was "over" at the NATO summit removed the last thread of diplomatic cover that markets had been clinging to since an interim accord in May.

"Wednesday was not a correction. It was a reversal," said Sarvam Goel, founder of Pocketful. "Everything markets celebrated over the past two months — cheaper crude, easing geopolitical risk, rate-cut hopes — all unravelled in a single session."

Brent crude surged 6.3 percent to around $79 a barrel, its highest level in two weeks. West Texas Intermediate climbed 5.2 percent to $74. Tehran revoked passage rights through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most critical oil chokepoints through which roughly 20 percent of global petroleum passes daily. Washington simultaneously pulled Iran's oil export licence, tightening the supply vise further.

## Why India gets hit harder

Higher oil prices are uniquely destructive for India, the world's third-largest oil importer and consumer. Nearly 85 percent of India's crude requirements are met through imports. When oil spikes, the cascading effects are immediate: a widening current account deficit, higher inflation through costlier fuel and transport, a weakening rupee, and a shrinking window for the Reserve Bank of India to cut interest rates — the very macro tailwinds that had powered the market's rally since April.

The Indian rupee weakened 0.62 percent to 95.55 against the US dollar, its lowest level in nearly a month. The RBI was reported to have intervened through dollar sales via state-run banks to limit the slide. The benchmark 10-year government bond yield rose more than 7 basis points to 6.77 percent, reflecting inflation expectations.

"Just when it looked like the macros were improving, Middle East uncertainty is back on the table," said a Mumbai-based bond trader. Another warned that "TACO trades" — the market shorthand for "Trump Always Chickens Out" — might not work as easily this time.

## The damage across sectors

The India VIX, the market's fear gauge, surged more than 26 percent — signalling a sharp spike in expected volatility. Market breadth was overwhelmingly negative, with declines outnumbering advances by nearly 4 to 1 across the BSE.

Among the biggest losers were oil marketing companies, airlines, paint manufacturers, and tyre stocks — all acutely sensitive to crude input costs. Jio Financial Services fell 3 percent, Max Healthcare dropped 2.2 percent, and Hindustan Unilever shed 2 percent. Mid-cap and small-cap indices fell 1.6 percent and 2.2 percent respectively, underperforming the frontline benchmarks.

On the limited bright side, a few defensive and export-oriented names eked out gains. Eternal (formerly Zomato) rose 2.2 percent, Bajaj Auto gained 1.3 percent, and Wipro added 1.1 percent.

Foreign institutional investors, who had turned net buyers over the previous three sessions — a development analysts had described as a "meaningful shift" — were widely expected to have reversed course in late trading as higher crude prices revived macroeconomic concerns.

## What NRI investors should watch

For NRI investors with Indian market exposure, the key variables in the coming sessions are clear. First, crude oil: if Brent sustains above $75 to $80, the entire macro case for India's second-half recovery comes under pressure. Second, the Strait of Hormuz: any sustained disruption to tanker traffic would send energy markets into a deeper spiral. Third, earnings season: TCS kicks off quarterly results on Thursday, July 10, and management commentary on US client spending will set the tone for the IT sector's rebound narrative.

"Until crude stabilises and the Strait situation clarifies, capital preservation is the only rational strategy," said Goel. "Wait. Watch. And then deploy."

Analysts at Axis Securities noted that while the near-term outlook has turned "neutral to cautious," the major demand zones remain intact, suggesting buying interest on deeper dips. The critical resistance zone of 24,500 to 24,600 on the Nifty, which markets had been approaching before today's sell-off, now looks considerably further away.
